project.description: Static review of the source tree trustwallet-wallet-core-en at adf80f8bac989e18a4ef1922e2b9eaeb4bf804a9. 1695 files analysed; of 2104 files, 373 are test, fuzzing, benchmark or example code and were left out, 35 are not read by any analyzer, 1 exceed the per-file limit and 0 did not fit the total limit. No requests were sent to the owner's systems.

decisions.note: wallet-core uses serde_with only in tw_zcash (PCZT transparent bundle) as serde_as(as = "BTreeMap<[_; 33], _>"); KeyValueMap, the type whose serialization panics, is not referenced anywhere in the tree.
time 0.3.44 is pulled in only by serde_with (Cargo.lock), which wallet-core uses only for the BTreeMap adapter above; the affected RFC 2822 parsing functions are not reached.

crypto-bigint 0.5.1 (multiple timing variability issues in operations intended to be constant-time) is a hard, non-optional dependency of the signing path, so unlike in the BitBox02 firmware there is no feature flag to hide behind. rust/tw_keypair/Cargo.toml declares k256 0.13.0 with features ["ecdh", "ecdsa", "pkcs8", "schnorr", "std"] and p256 0.13.0 with ["ecdsa", "std"], both of which depend on elliptic-curve, which depends on crypto-bigint; starknet-crypto and starknet-ff reach it directly as well. Traced in rust/Cargo.lock: the workspace roots tw_tests and wallet_core_bin both reach it, by way of tw_keypair and therefore of every chain crate that signs. This is a library that signs on behalf of wallets on a host operating system, so timing variability in operations documented as constant-time is in scope rather than academic. No exploit is demonstrated and the attacker needs local measurement; medium, not high. Fixed in crypto-bigint 0.7.6, which is a breaking upgrade through elliptic-curve and will need k256/p256 to move first.

Both affected versions are present (block-buffer 0.9.0 and 0.10.3) and both reach almost the whole tree through digest and blake-hash, so the dependency claim is right. The advisory needs a panic to be caught and the corrupted buffer then reused, and that cannot happen here: a code search for catch_unwind across trustwallet/wallet-core returns zero hits, and the C FFI boundary propagates rather than catches. The same advisory recurs in bitbox02-firmware, zcash's librustzcash, lightwalletd, zebra and the Android SDK, and monero-project/monero — which is the recurrence argument for a consolidated inventory, and is why it is worth recording a reasoned decision once rather than six times.

anyhow 1.0.75 (unsoundness in Error::downcast_mut) arrives through move-core-types, so only the Aptos and Sui crates depend on it, and no audited file calls downcast_mut. Upgrading to 1.0.103 is routine maintenance rather than a fix for an exposure here.

rand 0.8.5 is unsound only when a custom global logger calls rand::rng() reentrantly. wallet-core installs no global logger; rand reaches the tree through secp256k1, ark-std, fixed-hash and move-core-types, none of which log from inside the generator. The affected functions rand::rng and rand::thread_rng are not named in the audited code.

keccak 0.1.3's unsoundness is in the opt-in ARMv8 assembly backend behind the asm Cargo feature, which is off by default and which no manifest in the audited tree enables; the advisory's own CVSS vector (AV:L/AC:H/AT:P, exploit maturity unproven) reflects that. keccak arrives through sha3 and tw_hash, both using the portable implementation. Upgrading to 0.1.6 is routine maintenance.

Accurate as stated, and the reason it cannot simply be removed is worth recording. rust/tw_hash/src/sha1.rs defines sha1() and rust/tw_hash/src/ffi.rs:128 exports it over the C FFI; it is published through the library's public surface as TWHash (include/TrustWalletCore/TWHash.h, src/interface/TWHash.cpp, src/Hash.h, src/Hash.cpp). No in-tree security decision depends on it, which is exactly what the rule says. But src/Bitcoin/OpCodes.h references SHA-1 because Bitcoin Script defines OP_SHA1, so a wallet library that evaluates or builds scripts has to be able to compute it: this is a consensus-level requirement, not a choice the library can revisit. Correct disposition is therefore to keep it, document it as script-compatibility only, and ensure no new caller uses it for integrity — not to delete it.

Accurate: across 47 dependency manifests the declared cryptography is curve25519-dalek, ecdsa, k256, p256 and secp256k1, with nothing PQC-capable. For a library that signs for 43 chains this is not a dependency that can usefully be added yet — each chain's signature scheme is set by its own consensus, so until a chain defines a post-quantum scheme there is nothing for the wallet to implement against. The actionable part is the opposite direction: the library should be ready to carry two schemes per chain during a transition, which is an architectural question about tw_keypair rather than a missing crate.

Three advisories in two build-only crates (ansi_term 0.12.1 RUSTSEC-2021-0139; atty 0.2.14 GHSA-g98v-hv3f-hcfr and RUSTSEC-2024-0375), neither of which ships in a built artefact. They are worth updating during routine maintenance, and worth watching only insofar as they run in CI with credentials.

Five unmaintained-crate notices (bincode 1.3.3, derivative 2.2.0, paste 1.0.11, proc-macro-error 1.0.4, unsafe-libyaml 0.2.11). None reports a defect and none carries cryptography, so none bears on post-quantum readiness; recording the decision to keep them, which is what an informational advisory asks for.

Role resolved: trezor-crypto/crypto/bip32.c:710 is the vendored copy of trezor-crypto's hdnode_get_shared_key, the same ECDH-over-a-BIP-32-node function reviewed in trezor-firmware.yml. Session keys for identity and encryption features, so harvest-now-decrypt-later applies; one row, not a signing exposure.

Role resolved: all three anchors are the vendored trezor-crypto C library (trezor-crypto/crypto/bip32.c:504, crypto/ed25519-donna/ed25519.c, include/TrezorCrypto/ed25519.h) — the curve25519 public-key derivation layer underneath the Ed25519 signing rows, not an independent use. In the inventory because the derivation changes in any post-quantum scheme; not additional exposure on top of the signing rows.

Role resolved: the anchors are the keypair implementation itself — rust/tw_keypair/src/ecdsa/{mod.rs,nist256p1/private.rs,nist256p1/public.rs} and schnorr/public.rs — plus per-chain signature types (tw_binance/src/signature.rs, tw_internet_computer/src/protocol/principal.rs). This is the secp256k1 and NIST P-256 ECDSA that every chain crate signs through, so it is the same exposure as the transaction-signing rows reached one layer lower. Count it once: it is where the migration work lands, not an extra surface.

Role resolved: rust/tw_keypair/src/tw/{private,public}.rs are the type-erased keypair wrappers, and the remaining anchors are per-chain compilers and request builders (tw_pactus, tw_ton). Transaction signing, reached through the generic keypair layer rather than named at the call site — which is exactly why the role came back undetermined.

True by construction and the headline row for this repository: the protobuf definitions cover 43 chains, every one of which authorizes transactions with ECDSA, Ed25519 or Schnorr. A wallet library cannot migrate any of them unilaterally — consensus decides — so the deliverable is a per-chain readiness map, and its ordering is the actual product. Nothing here is a defect in wallet-core.

The remaining rows carry roles the engine determined and review agrees with. ECDSA across 84 files (211 references), anchored at include/TrustWalletCore/TWCurve.h:14 and running through every chain's signer, and Ed25519 across 33 files, are transaction and message signing: a CRQC derives the private key from a public key that is already on chain after the first spend. ECDSA at tw_internet_computer/src/protocol/identity.rs:6 is authentication and identity, a shorter-lived exposure. This repository is the largest single row count in the portfolio (355 inventory rows, 254 Shor-breakable) because it supports the most chains, not because it is the weakest code.

findings.title: Transaction signing for 43 chain(s) relies on elliptic-curve signatures
findings.description: The wallet's message definitions cover Aion, Algorand, Aptos, BNB Beacon Chain, BNB Greenfield, Bitcoin, Cardano, Cosmos SDK chains, Decred, EOS, Ethereum and EVM chains, Everscale, FIO, Filecoin, Harmony, Hedera, ICON, IOST, Internet Computer, IoTeX, MultiversX, NEAR, NULS, Nano, Nebulas, Neo, Nervos CKB, Nimiq, Oasis, Ontology, Polkadot and Substrate chains, Polymesh, Solana, Stellar, Sui, TON, Tezos, Theta, Tron, VeChain, XRP Ledger, Zcash (transparent), æternity. These chains authorize transactions with BLS12-381, ECDSA, Ed25519, Schnorr (BIP-340), sr25519, which Shor's algorithm breaks on a cryptographically relevant quantum computer. A wallet cannot move a chain to post-quantum signatures on its own: the chain has to adopt a scheme first.
findings.impact: Once a CRQC exists, an attacker who sees an account's public key could derive the private key and move funds; how soon keys are exposed depends on each chain (address reuse, account model).
findings.recommendation: Follow each chain's post-quantum roadmap, avoid public-key reuse, and keep signers ready to add post-quantum signature schemes as chains adopt them. Keep the signing layer crypto-agile per chain (algorithm identifiers in messages and storage, room for larger keys and signatures) and track each chain's post-quantum proposals, so that a new scheme can be added when a chain activates it.
findings.retest: Re-run when a chain activates a post-quantum signature scheme or the wallet adds one.
findings.limitations: This is a forward-looking risk that depends on the arrival of a cryptographically relevant quantum computer (CRQC). No such computer is publicly known to exist today; the timeline is uncertain. It is not a present-day exploitable vulnerability. Chains are recognized from the names of the message definitions (.proto files and packages); the schemes are the chains' documented account signatures, not an analysis of the wallet's signing code.
findings.method: Message definitions (.proto) matched to QSI's table of chain signature schemes.
findings.repro: Open the .proto files named in the evidence.

quantum_algorithms.name: Shor's algorithm — discrete logarithms in finite fields
quantum_algorithms.model_label: Q1: quantum computation offline, classical access to the victim
quantum_algorithms.audit: Breaks finite-field Diffie–Hellman and DSA at every size. Move key establishment to ML-KEM (hybrid with X25519 or ECDH during the transition) and signatures to ML-DSA or SLH-DSA.
quantum_algorithms.practicality: Gidney–Ekerå (2021) estimate RSA and finite-field discrete logarithms together; the resources are of the same order. Ekerå–Gärtner (2024) compare the current algorithm variants for safe-prime and Schnorr groups.

quantum_algorithms.name: Shor's algorithm — elliptic-curve discrete logarithms
quantum_algorithms.model_label: Q1: quantum computation offline, classical access to the victim
quantum_algorithms.audit: Elliptic-curve keys are expected to fall before RSA keys of comparable classical strength. On blockchains, coins whose public key is already on chain (reused addresses, pay-to-public-key and Taproot outputs) are exposed first; plan the move to post-quantum signatures and avoid key reuse in the meantime.
quantum_algorithms.practicality: 2026 estimates for a 256-bit curve: under 1,200 logical qubits and 90 million Toffoli gates, under half a million physical superconducting qubits running for minutes (Babbush et al.); 1,193 logical qubits with more gates (Chevignard–Fouque–Schrottenloher); P-256 in a few days on 26,000 neutral-atom qubits (Cain et al.). Scenarios under stated assumptions, not forecasts.

quantum_algorithms.name: Grover's algorithm — key search and preimages
quantum_algorithms.model_label: Q1: quantum computation offline, classical access to the victim
quantum_algorithms.audit: Not a break. 256-bit keys (AES-256, ChaCha20) keep a comfortable margin; AES-128 meets NIST category 1, while some authorities ask for 256-bit keys in quantum-resistant contexts (see the AES-128 entry). Prefer 256-bit keys for long-lived data; 256-bit hashes need no change for preimage resistance.
quantum_algorithms.practicality: The search is long and serial: NIST counts AES-128 key search as 2^170/MAXDEPTH quantum gates with MAXDEPTH between 2^40 and 2^96 and uses it as the yardstick of security category 1; a SHA-256 preimage was estimated at about 2^153.8 surface-code cycles on 2^12.6 logical qubits (Amy et al. 2016).

quantum_algorithms.name: Brassard–Høyer–Tapp — collision search
quantum_algorithms.model_label: Q1: quantum computation offline, classical access to the victim
quantum_algorithms.audit: 256-bit hashes (SHA-256, SHA3-256) remain adequate for collision resistance; 160-bit hashes are already weak classically (SHA-1 collisions are practical). Use 384/512-bit hashes where NIST categories 4–5 are required.
quantum_algorithms.practicality: Bernstein (2009) argued that, once hardware cost is counted, it is not cheaper than classical parallel collision search; NIST defines security category 2 by SHA3-256 collision search counted in classical gates (2^146).

scenario.rationale: Inside the 10-year horizon the survey puts at 28-49% ('quite possible'), and consistent with the BSI estimate of 15 years that 'could shrink to 10 or even less'. Use it for data that must stay confidential for decades, where being wrong is expensive.
